entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1-Gen.35.7">Gen 35:1-7</reference> <hi type="italic">Journey to Bethel</hi>. - Jacob had allowed ten years to pass since his return from Mesopotamia, without performing the vow which he made at Bethel when fleeing from Esau (Gen 28:20.), although he had recalled it to mind when resolving to return (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.13">Gen 31:13</reference>), and had also erected an altar in Shechem to the “God of Israel” (<reference osisRef="Gen.33.20">Gen 33:20</reference>). He was now directed by God (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference>) to go to Bethel, and there build an altar to the God who had appeared to him on his flight from Esau. This command stirred him up to perform what had been neglected, viz., to put away from his house the strange gods, which he had tolerated in weak consideration for his wives, and which had no doubt occasioned the long neglect, and to pay to God the vow that he had made in the day of his trouble. He therefore commanded his house (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.2">Gen 35:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.3">Gen 35:3</reference>), i.e., his wives and children, and “<hi type="italic">all that were with him,</hi>” i.e., his men and maid-servants, to put away the strange gods, to purify themselves, and wash their clothes. He also buried “all the strange gods,” i.e., Rachel’s teraphim (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.19">Gen 31:19</reference>), and whatever other idols there were, with the earrings which were worn as amulets and charms, “<hi type="italic">under the terebinth at Shechem,</hi>” probably the very tree under which Abraham once pitched his tent (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Gen 12:6</reference>), and which was regarded as a sacred place in Joshua’s time (vid., <reference osisRef="Josh.24.26">Jos 24:26</reference>, though the pointing is אלּה there). The burial of the idols was followed by purification through the washing of the body, as a sign of the purification of the heart from the defilement of idolatry, and by the putting on of clean and festal clothes, as a symbol of the sanctification and elevation of the heart to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.23">Jos 24:23</reference>). This decided turning to the Lord was immediately followed by the blessing of God. When they left Shechem a “<hi type="italic">terror of God,</hi>” i.e., a supernatural terror, “<hi type="italic">came upon the cities round about,</hi>” so that they did not venture to pursue the sons of Jacob on account of the cruelty of Simeon and Levi (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.5">Gen 35:5</reference>). Having safely arrived in Bethel, Jacob built an altar, which he called <hi type="italic">El Bethel</hi> (God of Bethel) in remembrance of the manifestation of God on His flight from Esau.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.35.8">Gen 35:8</reference> <div eID="gen412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen413" type="x-p"/> There <hi type="italic">Deborah</hi>, Rebekah’s nurse, died, and was buried below Bethel under an oak, which was henceforth called the “oak of weeping,” a mourning oak, from the grief of Jacob’s house on account of her death. Deborah had either been sent by Rebekah to take care of her daughters-in-law and grandsons, or had gone of her own accord into Jacob’s household after the death of her mistress. The mourning at her death, and the perpetuation of her memory, are proofs that she must have been a faithful and highly esteemed servant in Jacob’s house.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.35.9-Gen.35.15">Gen 35:9-15</reference> <div eID="gen413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen414" type="x-p"/> The Fresh Revelation at Bethel. - After Jacob had performed his vow by erecting the altar at Bethel, God appeared to him again there (“<hi type="italic">again,</hi>” referring to Gen 28), “<hi type="italic">on his coming out of Padan-Aram,</hi>” as He had appeared to him 30 years before on his journey thither, - though it was then in a dream, now by daylight in a visible form (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.35.13">Gen 35:13</reference>, “<hi type="italic">God went up from him</hi>”). The gloom of that day of fear had now brightened into the clear daylight of salvation. This appearance was the answer, which God gave to Jacob on his acknowledgement of Him; and its reality is thereby established, in opposition to the conjecture that it is merely a legendary repetition of the previous vision.<note placement="foot">This conjecture derives no support from the fact that the manifestations of God are ascribed to <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference> and Gen 35:9., although the whole chapter treats of the display of mercy by the covenant God, i.e., <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>. For the occurrence of <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference> may be explained, partly from the antithesis of God and man (because <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi>, the man, had neglected to redeem his vow, it was necessary that he should be reminded of it by God), and partly from the fact that there is no allusion to any <hi type="italic">appearance</hi> of God, but the words “God said” are to be understood, no doubt, as relating to an inward communication. The use of <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in Gen 35:9. follows naturally from the injunction of <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference>; and there was the less necessity for an express designation of the God appearing as <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, because, on the one hand, the object of this appearance was simply to renew and confirm the former appearance of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> (Gen 28:12.), and on the other hand, the title assumed in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.11">Gen 35:11</reference>, <hi type="italic">El Shaddai</hi>, refers to <reference osisRef="Gen.27.1">Gen 27:1</reference>, where <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> announces Himself to Abram as <hi type="italic">El Shaddai</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen415" type="x-p"/> The former theophany had promised to Jacob divine protection in a foreign land and restoration to his home, on the ground of his call to be the bearer of the blessings of salvation. This promise God had fulfilled, and Jacob therefore performed his vow. On the strength of this, God now confirmed to him the name of Israel, which He had already given him in <reference osisRef="Gen.32.28">Gen 32:28</reference>, and with it the promised of a numerous seed and the possession of Canaan, which, so far as the form and substance are concerned, points back rather to <reference osisRef="Gen.17.6">Gen 17:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.17.8">Gen 17:8</reference> than to <reference osisRef="Gen.28.13-Gen.28.14">Gen 28:13-14</reference>, and for the fulfilment of which, commencing with the birth of his sons and his return to Canaan, and stretching forward to the most remote future, the name of <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> was to furnish him with a pledge. - Jacob alluded to this second manifestation of God at Bethel towards the close of his life (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.3-Gen.48.4">Gen 48:3-4</reference>); and Hosea (Hos 12:4) represents it as the result of his wrestling with God. The remembrance of this appearance Jacob transmitted to his descendants by erecting a memorial stone, which he not only anointed with oil like the former one in <reference osisRef="Gen.28.17">Gen 28:17</reference>, but consecrated by a drink-offering and by the renewal of the name Bethel.

Gen 35:9-15

Gen 35:13, “God went up from him”). The gloom of that day of fear had now brightened into the clear daylight of salvation. This appearance was the answer, which God gave to Jacob on his acknowledgement of Him; and its reality is thereby established, in opposition to the conjecture that it is merely a legendary repetition of the previous vision.This conjecture derives no support from the fact that the manifestations of God are ascribed to Elohim in Gen 35:1 and Gen 35:9., although the whole chapter treats of the display of mercy by the covenant God, i.e., Jehovah.  The former theophany had promised to Jacob divine protection in a foreign land and restoration to his home, on the ground of his call to be the bearer of the blessings of salvation. This promise God had fulfilled, and Jacob therefore performed his vow. On the strength of this, God now confirmed to him the name of Israel, which He had already given him in Gen 32:28, and with it the promised of a numerous seed and the possession of Canaan, which, so far as the form and substance are concerned, points back rather to Gen 17:6 and Gen 17:8 than to Gen 28:13-14, and for the fulfilment of which, commencing with the birth of his sons and his return to Canaan, and stretching forward to the most remote future, the name of Israel was to furnish him with a pledge. - Jacob alluded to this second manifestation of God at Bethel towards the close of his life (Gen 48:3-4); and Hosea (Hos 12:4) represents it as the result of his wrestling with God. The remembrance of this appearance Jacob transmitted to his descendants by erecting a memorial stone, which he not only anointed with oil like the former one in Gen 28:17, but consecrated by a drink-offering and by the renewal of the name Bethel.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.35.16-Gen.35.20">Gen 35:16-20</reference> <div eID="gen415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen416" type="x-p"/> Birth of Benjamin and Death of Rachel. - Jacob’s departure from Bethel was not in opposition to the divine command, “dwell there” (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.1">Gen 35:1</reference>). For the word שׁב does not enjoin a permanent abode; but, when taken in connection with what follows, “make there an altar,” it merely directs him to stay there and perform his vow. As they were travelling forward, Rachel was taken in labour not far from Ephratah. הארץ כּברת is a space, answering probably to the Persian parassang, though the real meaning of כּברה is unknown. The birth was a difficult one. בּלדתּהּ תּקשׁ: she had difficulty in her labour (instead of <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> we find <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.35.17">Gen 35:17</reference> with the same signification). The midwife comforted her by saying: “<hi type="italic">Fear not, for this also is to thee a son,</hi>” - a wish expressed by her when Joseph was born (<reference osisRef="Gen.30.24">Gen 30:24</reference>). But she expired; and as she was dying, she called him <hi type="italic">Been-oni</hi>, “son of my pain.” Jacob, however, called him <hi type="italic">Ben-jamin</hi>, probably son of good fortune, according to the meaning of the word <hi type="italic">jamin</hi> sustained by the Arabic, to indicate that his pain at the loss of his favourite wife was compensated by the birth of this son, who now completed the number twelve. Other explanations are less simple. He buried Rachel on the road to Ephratah, or Ephrath (probably the fertile, from פּרה), i.e., Bethlehem (bread-house), by which name it is better known, though the origin of it is obscure. He also erected a monument over her grave (מצּבה, στήλη), on which the historian observes, “<hi type="italic">This is the pillar of Rachel’s grave unto this day:</hi>” a remark which does not necessarily point to a post-Mosaic period, but which could easily have been made even 10 or 20 years after its erection. For the fact that a grave-stone had been preserved upon the high road in a foreign land, the inhabitants of which had no interest whatever in it, might appear worthy of notice even though only a single decennary had passed away.<note placement="foot">But even if this <hi type="italic">Mazzebah</hi> was really preserved till the conquest of Canaan by the Israelites, i.e., more than 450 years, and the remark referred to that time, it might be an interpolation by a later hand. The grave was certainly a well-known spot in Samuel’s time (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>); but a <hi type="italic">monumentum ubi Rachel posita est uxor Jacob</hi> is first mentioned again by the Bordeaux pilgrims of a.d. 333 and <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Kubbet Rahil</hi> (Rachel’s grave), which is now shown about half an hour’s journey to the north of Bethlehem, to the right of the road from Jerusalem to Hebron, is merely “an ordinary Muslim wely, or tomb of a holy person, a small square building of stone with a dome, and within it a tomb in the ordinary Mohammedan form” (Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> 1, p. 322). It has been recently enlarged by a square court with high walls and arches on the eastern side (Rob. <hi type="italic">Bibl. Researches.</hi> p. 357). Now although this grave is not ancient, the correctness of the tradition, which fixes upon this as the site of Rachel’s grave, cannot on the whole be disputed. At any rate, the reasons assigned to the contrary by <hi type="italic">Thenius</hi>, <hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi>, and others are not conclusive.</note>

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.35.21-Gen.35.22">Gen 35:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen417" type="x-p"/> Reuben’s Incest. - As they travelled onward, Jacob pitched his tent on the other side of <hi type="italic">Migdal Eder</hi>, where Reuben committed incest with Bilhah, his father’s concubine. It is merely alluded to her in the passing remark that Israel heard it, by way of preparation for Gen 49:4. <hi type="italic">Migdal Eder</hi> (flock-tower) was a watch-tower built for the protection of flocks against robbers (cf. 2Ki 18:8; <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.10">2Ch 26:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.27.4">2Ch 27:4</reference>) on the other side of Bethlehem, but hardly within 1000 paces of the town, where it has been placed by tradition since the time of Jerome. The <hi type="italic">piska</hi> in the middle of <reference osisRef="Gen.35.22">Gen 35:22</reference> does not indicate a gap in the text, but the conclusion of a <hi type="italic">parashah</hi>, a division of the text of greater antiquity and greater correctness than the Masoretic division.
